verses.zh: 亚摩斯的儿子以赛亚得默示，论到犹大和耶路撒冷。
verses.en: Here is the message about Judah and Jerusalem[NOTE:1] that was revealed to Isaiah son of Amoz.[NOTE:2]
notes: For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
Heb “the word which Isaiah son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem.”
verses.commentary:
2:1 It is uncertain why Isaiah's messages are described as

- a vision, Isa. 1:1; 29:7 (BDB 302, cf. Micah 3:6)

- he saw, Isa. 1:1; 2:1; 13:1; 26:11; 33:17; 48:6; 57:8 (cf. Micah 1:1)

This is the mystery of revelation. It comes in different ways to different biblical authors
(visions, dreams, theophanies, words, etc.). Moderns do not know how much freedom the individual writers
(authors, editors, compilers) had to structure and present God's message. They obviously used their own
language skills and vocabularies. Even without a full and complete understanding of the way revelation works,
the concept is crucial! These are God's messages given through a historically conditioned person, to a
particular time and group, yet they are relevant for all people in all times! The key for a proper
interpretation is that the intent of an original inspired author must be the
criteria for interpretation (one meaning but many significances/applications).

A good book that has helped me deal with the cultural particularity of Scripture is
Gordon Fee, Gospel and Spirit. Another good book that helps identify and deal with different biblical
genres is Fee and Stuart, How To Read the Bible for All Its Worth, ISBN 0-310-24604-0

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

▣ "the son of Amoz" See note at Isa. 1:1.

verses.zh: 末后的日子，耶和华殿的山必坚立，超乎诸山，高举过于万岭；万民都要流归这山。
verses.en: In future days[NOTE:1] the mountain of the Lord’s temple will endure[NOTE:2] as the most important of mountainsand will be the most prominent of hills.[NOTE:3] All the nations will stream to it;
notes: The verse begins with a verb that functions as a “discourse particle” and is not translated. In numerous places throughout the OT, the “to be” verb with a prefixed conjunction (וְהָיָה [vehayah] and וַיְהִי [vayehi]) occurs in this fashion to introduce a circumstantial clause and does not require translation.sn “In future days” refers generally to the future, but here and in Micah 4:1 it may also refer to the final period of history (see the note at Gen 49:1).
Or “be established” (KJV, NIV, NRSV).

Heb “as the chief of the mountains, and will be lifted up above the hills.” The image of Mount Zion being elevated above other mountains and hills pictures the prominence it will attain in the future.
verses.commentary:
2:2-4 This brief paragraph summarizes the OT perspective on the place and purpose of the covenant people
(similar to Micah 4:1-5). They were to be a light to the nations (cf. Isa. 51:4,5; Matt. 28:18-20; Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8)!

The Jewish Study Bible calls vv. 2-4 "one of the most famous texts in the Bible," p. 787.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

2:2 "In the last days" This phrase refers to the future horizon of the particular biblical writer
(see G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, chapter 14, "The Language of Eschatology,"
pp. 243-271). It denoted a time of fulfillment of God's purposes.

- the Messianic kingdom, Gen. 49:1-27 (esp. 49:10); Num. 24:14-25 (esp. 24:17); Isa. 2:2;
Jer. 48:47; 49:39; Ezek. 38:8,16

- Israel's rebellion, Deut. 31:29

- Israel's return to YHWH in repentance and faith, Deut. 4:30; Hosea 3:5; Jer. 23:19-22 (esp. 23:20)

- an end-time attack on the covenant people, Ezek. 38:16; Dan. 2:28; 10:14 (possibly Psalm 2)

- exile, Amos 4:2

Only context can clarify which period. Be careful of your systematic theology!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE LAST DAYS

SPECIAL TOPIC: THIS AGE AND THE AGE TO COME

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE MESSIANIC ERA

▣ "The mountain of the house of the Lord" This refers to the temple
located on Mt. Moriah in Jerusalem. It was the place of centralized worship of YHWH (the place He caused
His name to dwell, cf. Deut. 12:5,11,14,18,21,26; 14:25; 15:20; 16:2,6,11,15; 17:8,10; 18:6; 26:2; 31:11).

The NIV Study Bible (pp. 962-3) comments how common in Isaiah is the theme of the
mountain of the Lord where all the nations come in the last days
(cf. Isa. 11:9; 27:13; 56:7; 57:13; 65:25; 66:20).

In a sense this elevation of Mt. Zion (i.e. Jerusalem, the site of the temple of YHWH) is
depicted in Canaanite myth (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 4, pp. 1314-1321). For the Canaanites the gods dwelt on
Mt. Zaphon in the far north (cf. Isa. 14:13), but Ps. 48:2 changes the imagery to Mt. Zion. YHWH is
above all Canaanite deities!

This same concept of a temple or a city being raised is also found in Mesopotamian literature
(cf. The Weidner Chronicle, Assyrian inscriptions, Marduk Prophecy). So the concept is not unique to Isaiah.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MORIAH, SALEM, JEBUS, JERUSALEM, ZION

▣ Notice the metaphorical language used to describe the chief place of YHWH's revelation to
Abraham's descendants.

- "the chief of the mountains," i.e. the place of true revelation

- "raised above the hills," a symbol of preeminence and exclusiveness

- "all the nations will stream to it," this has always been YHWH's goal, cf. Gen. 3:15; 12:3;
Exod. 19:5-6; Ps. 22:27; 66:1-4; 86:8-10; Isa. 2:2-4; 12:4-5; 25:6-9; 42:6-12; 45:22-23;
49:5-6; 51:4-5; 56:6-8; 60:1-3; 66:23; Jer. 3:17; Micah 4:1-4; Mal. 1:11; John 3:16; 4:42; Acts 10:34-35;
1 Tim. 2:4; Titus 2:11; 2 Pet. 3:9; 1 John 2:2; 4:14! This is the natural result of monotheism.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHY ARE THE END-TIME EVENTS SO CONTROVERSIAL?

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

▣ "all the nations will stream to it" This VERB (BDB 625, KB 676,
Qal PERFECT with waw) denotes an ever-flowing stream of water,
like an artesian well. Here, it is imagery for the unending flow of the nations to YHWH
(i.e. Isa. 56:6-8).

verses.zh: 必有许多国的民前往，说：来吧，我们登耶和华的山，奔雅各　神的殿。主必将他的道教训我们；我们也要行他的路。因为训诲必出于锡安；耶和华的言语必出于耶路撒冷。
verses.en: many peoples will come and say,“Come, let us go up to the Lord’s mountain,to the temple of the God of Jacob,so[NOTE:1] he can teach us his requirements,[NOTE:2] and[NOTE:3] we can follow his standards.”[NOTE:4] For Zion will be the center for moral instruction;[NOTE:5] the Lord’s message will issue from Jerusalem.
notes: The prefixed verb form with simple vav (ו) introduces a purpose/result clause after the preceding prefixed verb form (probably to be taken as a cohortative; see IBHS 650 §39.2.2a).
Heb “his ways.” In this context God’s “ways” are the standards of moral conduct he decrees that people should live by.
The cohortative with vav (ו) after the prefixed verb form indicates the ultimate purpose/goal of their action.
Heb “walk in his ways.”
Heb “for out of Zion will go instruction.”
verses.commentary:
2:3 The JPSOA translates "will stream to it" as "will gaze on it with joy." Originally the priests and Levites were to be the teachers of the Law (cf. Deut. 31:9; 33:10). People
who wanted to know YHWH and His will would come to the temple (i.e. both Israelites and Gentiles, cf. 1 Kgs. 8:43,60;
Isa. 57:6; Mark 11:17).

Notice the request of the nations.

- "come,"BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERATIVE

- "let us go up to the mountain of the Lord," BDB 748,
KB 828, Qal IMPERFECT used in a COHORTATIVE
sense

- "That He may teach us concerning His ways," BDB 434, KB 436, Hiphil
IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

- "that we may walk in His paths," BDB 229, KB 246, Qal COHORTATIVE
(see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY)

- "that the law (teachings) will go forth from Zion," BDB 422, KB 425, Qal
IMPERFECT used in a COHORTATIVE sense (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS FOR GOD'S REVELATION)

▣ "Lord. . .God" The first title/name is YHWH, the covenant
name for Israel's Deity, first used in Gen. 2:4.

The second title/name is Eloah, which is the SINGULAR form of
Elohim, or possibly for El, the God of creation from Gen. 1:1.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, A., C., D.

▣ "His paths" This term (BDB 73) is used several times in Isaiah (cf. Isa. 2:3; 3:12;
26:7,8; 30:11; 33:8; 40:18; 41:3) and prominently in Proverbs (cf. Isa. 1:19; 2:8,13,15,19,20; 3:6;
4:14,18; 5:6; 8:20; 9:15; 10:17; 12:28; 15:10,19,24; 17:23; 22:25). It is imagery to denote a
lifestyle faith that obeys and walks in God's teachings (cf. Exod. 16:4; Isa. 30:20; 42:24; Jer. 9:12; 26:4; 32:23;
44:10,23; Zech 7:12).

This imagery for lifestyle, faithful living became the first title of the NT church, "The Way"
(cf. John 14:6; Acts 9:2; 19:9,23; 22:4; 24:14,22; 18:25-26).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

▣ "Zion" Jerusalem (like Rome) was built on seven hills. Zion (BDB 851, KB 1022, meaning uncertain,
but KB's suggestions from an Arabic root are

- citadel

- barren place

- or bare hill)

was the hill on which the original Canaanite city of Jebus or Salem was built (cf. 1 Kgs. 8:1; 2 Chr. 5:2).
As Jerusalem grew it became a way of referring to the whole city and temple (cf. Isa. 2:3, lines 6 and 7;
Jer. 50:28: 51:10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ZION

verses.zh: 他必在列国中施行审判，为许多国民断定是非。他们要将刀打成犁头，把枪打成镰刀。这国不举刀攻击那国；他们也不再学习战事。
verses.en: He will judge disputes between nations;he will settle cases for many peoples.They will beat their swords into plowshares,[NOTE:1] and their spears into pruning hooks.[NOTE:2] Nations will not take up the sword against other nations,and they will no longer train for war.
notes: Instead of referring to the large plow as a whole, the plowshare is simply the metal tip which actually breaks the earth and cuts the furrow.

This implement was used to prune the vines, i.e., to cut off extra leaves and young shoots (H. Wildberger, Isaiah, 1:93; M. Klingbeil, NIDOTTE 1:1117-18). It was a short knife with a curved hook at the end sharpened on the inside like a sickle. Breaking weapons and fashioning agricultural implements indicates a transition from fear and stress to peace and security.
verses.commentary:
2:4 "He will judge. . .render decisions" These two VERBS (BDB 1047, KB 1622,
Qal PERFECT with waw and BDB 406, KB 410, Hiphil
PERFECT with waw) describe the reasonings and decisions of a wise ruler.
YHWH and His Messiah are the ultimate wise rulers (cf. Isa. 11:1-5; Mic. 5:4)!

▣ The Lord's presence and teachings will cause the
nations to abandon their attacks on His people (cf. Psalm 2; Ezekiel 38-39). They will pursue peace
(cf. Isa. 9:6-7; 11:6-9; 57:19; Hosea 2:18; Zech. 9:10).

▣ "swords into plowshares" This is an idiom for peace. The opposite occurs in Joel 3:10, where
it is an idiom for war.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE AND WAR

verses.zh: 雅各家啊，来吧！我们在耶和华的光明中行走。
verses.en: O descendants[NOTE:1] of Jacob,come, let us walk in the Lord’s guiding light.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “house,” referring to the family line or descendants (likewise in v. 6).

Heb “let’s walk in the light of the Lord.” In this context, which speaks of the Lord’s instruction and commands, the “light of the Lord” refers to his moral standards by which he seeks to guide his people. One could paraphrase, “let’s obey the Lord’s commands.”
verses.commentary:
2:5 Notice the parallel between Isa. 2:3 (the nations) and Isa. 2:5 (the Israelites). Lifestyle faith
is the evidence of a personal, trusting relationship with God. Humans must know the truth, walk in the truth,
and share it with others! The nations were to learn this from Israel, but they did not!

The "light of the Lord" is imagery for true revelation (cf. Isa. 60:1-2,19-20).
The worship of the lights of the night sky is false revelation. This verse may be a rejection of Babylonian
astral worship (cf. Isa. 2:6). YHWH and His Messiah are the true light for the nations (cf. Isa. 9:2; 42:6;
49:6; 51:4; 53:11).

verses.zh: 耶和华，你离弃了你百姓雅各家，是因他们充满了东方的风俗，作观兆的，像非利士人一样，并与外邦人击掌。
verses.en: Indeed, O Lord,[NOTE:1] you have abandoned your people,the descendants of Jacob.For diviners from the east are everywhere;[NOTE:2] they consult omen readers like the Philistines do.[NOTE:3] Plenty of foreigners are around.[NOTE:4]
notes: The words “O Lord” are supplied in the translation for clarification. Isaiah addresses the Lord in prayer.

Heb “they are full from the east.” Various scholars retain the BHS reading and suggest that the prophet makes a general statement concerning Israel’s reliance on foreign customs (J. Watts, Isaiah [WBC], 1:32; J. de Waard, Isaiah, 12-13). Nevertheless, it appears that a word is missing. Based on the parallelism (note “omen readers” in 2:6c), many suggest that קֹסְמִים (qosemim, “diviners”) or מִקְסָם (miqsam, “divination”) has been accidentally omitted. Homoioteleuton could account for the omission of an original קֹסְמִים (note how this word and the following מִקֶּדֶם [miqqedem, “from the east”] both end in mem); an original מִקְסָם could have fallen out by homoioarcton (note how this word and the following מִקֶּדֶם both begin with mem).

Heb “and omen readers like the Philistines.” Through this line and the preceding, the prophet contends that Israel has heavily borrowed the pagan practices of the east and west (in violation of Lev 19:26; Deut 18:9-14).

Heb “and with the children of foreigners they [?].” The precise meaning of the final word is uncertain. Some take this verb (I שָׂפַק, safaq) to mean “slap,” supply the object “hands,” and translate, “they slap [hands] with foreigners”; HALOT 1349 s.v. I שׂפק. This could be a reference to foreign alliances. This translation has two disadvantages: It requires the conjectural insertion of “hands” and the use of this verb with its object prefixed with a בְּ (bet) preposition with this meaning does not occur elsewhere. The other uses of this verb refer to clapping at someone, an indication of hostility. The translation above assumes the verb is derived from II שׂפק (“to suffice,” attested in the Qal in 1 Kgs 20:10; HALOT 1349 s.v. II שׂפק). In this case the point is that a sufficient number of foreigners (in this case, too many!) live in the land. The disadvantage of this option is that the preposition prefixed to “the children of foreigners” does not occur with this verb elsewhere. The chosen translation is preferred since it continues the idea of abundant foreign influence and does not require a conjectural insertion or emendation.
verses.commentary:
2:6-9 These verses describe why YHWH abandoned (BDB 643, KB 695, Qal
PERFECT) His own covenant people.

- They are filled with influence from the east, Isa. 2:6.

- They are soothsayers (BDB 778 II), like the Philistines, Isa. 2:6.

- They strike bargains with the children of foreigners, Isa. 2:6.

- They are wealthy and militarily strong (and trust in these things), Isa. 2:7 (notice the three-fold
repetition of "filled," BDB 569, KB 583, Niphal IMPERFECT with
waw in Isa. 2:7 and 8).

- They are idolatrous, Isa. 2:8 (cf. Isa. 17:8; 37:19; 40:19; 44:17).

- They treat the common people with disdain, Isa. 2:9 (cf. Isa. 2:11,17; it is possible that this
verse is parallel to Isa. 2:8 and refers to idolatry, cf. NKJV).

What can the nations learn from people like this?!

Concerning #6 above (Isa. 2:9), the NASB and NKJV translate it as another in a series
of descriptions of how the covenant people are acting, but NRSV and TEV translate it as a summary and
the last line is a plea for YHWH, not to forgive them (Peshitta) or a statement by YHWH that He will
not forgive them (LXX).

2:6

NASB, NRSV
"from the east"

NKJV
"eastern ways"

TEV, JPSOA
"from the East"

Peshitta
"olden days"

REB
"traders"

The UBS Hebrew OT Text Project gives "from the east" or "from olden times" (both
possible meanings of this NOUN, BDB 869, KB 1069) a "B" rating (some doubt). The NEB
and REB add one consonant and make it "traders." It seems to refer to religious influences (pagan idol worship)
from the east (i.e. Syria, Assyria, Babylon, see RSV) which corrupted Israel's faith.

▣ "soothsayers" If this was meant to be a strict parallelism with the line above, it is possible
that a NOUN parallel to "soothsayer" (BDB 778 II), such as "diviners" (cf. Lev. 19:26; Deut. 18:9-12; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: DIVINATION),
has inadvertently dropped out of the MT. The MT is not the earliest Hebrew text. It does
have textual problems! However, remember that these kinds of problems do not affect major doctrines.

NASB
"they strike bargains with the children of foreigners"

NKJV
"they are pleased with the children of foreigners"

NRSV
"they clasp hands with foreigners"

TEV
"they follow foreign customs"

NJB
"is overrun with foreigners"

LXX
"many strange children were born to them"

Peshitta
"they reared many alien children"

REB
"the children of foreigners are everywhere"

JPSOA
"they abound in customs of the aliens"

The term "children" is not in the MT. The VERB "they strike hands"
(i.e. make bargains, BDB 706 I, KB 765, Hiphil IMPERFECT) is ambiguous. It can refer to

- a commercial transaction

- a political alliance

- a friendship

- an affirmation of the customs of foreigners

Obviously in context the unique faith of Israel is being compromised!

verses.zh: 他们的国满了金银，财宝也无穷；他们的地满了马匹，车辆也无数。
verses.en: Their land is full of gold and silver;there is no end to their wealth.[NOTE:1] Their land is full of horses;there is no end to their chariots.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “treasuries”; KJV “treasures.”
Judah’s royal bureaucracy had accumulated great wealth and military might, in violation of Deut 17:16-17.
verses.commentary:
2:7 This description of Judean leadership is in direct contradiction to Deut. 17:16-17. Humans who
have resources tend to trust in them (cf. Isa. 31:1), but Isa. 2:22 (cf. Isa. 31:3) shows the failure of
trusting in physical or human resources (i.e. wealth and military equipment).

verses.zh: 他们的地满了偶像；他们跪拜自己手所造的，就是自己指头所做的。
verses.en: Their land is full of worthless idols;they worship[NOTE:1] the product of their own hands,what their own fingers have fashioned.
notes: Or “bow down to” (NIV, NRSV).

verses.zh: 卑贱人屈膝；尊贵人下跪；所以不可饶恕他们。
verses.en: Men bow down to them in homage,they lie flat on the ground in worship.[NOTE:1] Don’t spare them![NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “men bow down, men are low.” Since the verbs שָׁחָח (shakhakh) and שָׁפַל (shafal) are used later in this discourse to describe how God will humiliate proud men (see vv. 11, 17), some understand v. 9a as a prediction of judgment, “men will be brought down, men will be humiliated.” However, these prefixed verbal forms with vav (ו) consecutive appear to carry on the description that precedes and are better taken with the accusation. They draw attention to the fact that human beings actually bow down and worship before the lifeless products of their own hands.

Heb “don’t lift them up.” The idiom “lift up” (נָשָׂא with לְ, nasaʾ with preposition lamed) can mean “spare, forgive” (see Gen 18:24, 26). Here the idiom plays on the preceding verbs. The idolaters are bowed low as they worship their false gods; the prophet asks God not to “lift them up.”
verses.commentary:
2:9 "man. . .man" Isaiah 2:9 is a two-line, synonymous parallelism (cf. 2 Kgs. 7:10). The two most
common terms for mankind are parallel.

- adam, BDB 9, KB 14, cf. Gen. 1:26; 6:1,5,6,7; 9:5,6

- ish, BDB 35, KB 43, Gen. 2:23; Num. 23:19

See Robert Girdlestone, Synonyms of the Old Testament for "Adam," pp. 45-48 and
for "ish," pp. 48-50.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, TEV, JPSOA
"do not forgive them"

NJB, NIV
"do not raise them again"

LXX
"do not pardon them"

REB
(omits as gloss, cf. Dead Sea Scroll and JB footnote)

The VERB (BDB 669, KB 724, Qal
IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense) means
"to lift" or "to carry." Here it has the sense of "carry away" (i.e. remove their sin). This may
be an exclamation from Isaiah, himself.

This VERB (in Hebrew and Greek) is such an important and wonderful action.

- God will forgive sin ‒ Isa. 33:24

- Christ takes away sin ‒ John 1:29; 1 John 3:5

- carried/bore ‒ Isa. 53:4; Matt. 8:17; 1 Pet. 2:24

In this context, it is negated. The prophet asks that YHWH does not act on behalf of these flagrant covenant violators.

The footnote of JPSOA suggests an emendation to "and their idols with them," from vv. 17-21 (p.788).

verses.zh: 你当进入岩穴，藏在土中，躲避耶和华的惊吓和他威严的荣光。
verses.en: Go up into the rocky cliffs,hide in the ground.Get away from the dreadful judgment of the Lord,[NOTE:1] from his royal splendor!
notes: Heb “from the dread of the Lord,” that is, from the dread that he produces in the objects of his judgment.” The words “get away” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
verses.commentary:
2:10-11 These two verses describe YHWH's advice to these covenant violators (Isa. 2:10a).

- enter the rock, BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERATIVE (i.e. this relates
to Isa. 2:19-21, and possibly refers to caves or manmade tunnels, cf. Rev. 6:15-17)

- hide in the dust, BDB 380, KB 377, Niphal IMPERATIVE

They are to hide from (Isa. 2:10b)

- the terror of the Lord, cf. Isa. 2:19,21

- the splendor of His majesty (cf. Isa. 2:11c, 19,21; 2 Thess. 1:9)

The result will be (Isa. 2:11, note parallel in Isa. 2:17)

- the proud look of men will be abased, BDB 1050, KB 1631, Qal PERFECT
(opposite of Isa. 2:9)

- the loftiness of man will be humbled, BDB 1005, KB 1458, Qal PERFECT with
waw (opposite of Isa. 2:9, cf. Isa. 13:11; 23:9; 2 Cor. 10:5)

- the Lord alone will be exalted in that day, BDB 960, KB 1305, Niphal
PERFECT with waw (note parallel in Isa. 2:17 and the phrase about the
"terror" and "splendor" of YHWH in Isa. 2:19c and 21b)

Some commentators think that Isa. 2:10 is encouraging the righteous to hide from YHWH's
coming judgment on the wicked (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 377), but in context (i.e. Isa. 2:19-21) it refers
to the covenant violators.

verses.zh: 到那日，眼目高傲的必降为卑；性情狂傲的都必屈膝；惟独耶和华被尊崇。
verses.en: Proud men will be brought low,arrogant men will be humiliated;[NOTE:1] the Lord alone will be exalted[NOTE:2] in that day.
notes: Heb “and the eyes of the pride of men will be brought low, and the arrogance of men will be brought down.” The repetition of the verbs שָׁפַל (shafal) and שָׁחָח (shakhakh) from v. 9 draws attention to the appropriate nature of the judgment. Those proud men who “bow low” before idols will be forced to “bow low” before God when he judges their sin.
Or “elevated”; CEV “honored.”
verses.commentary:
2:11 "in that day" This refers to the last days of Isa. 2:2a. It becomes a dominate theme in Amos. The
theme in Isaiah is resumed in Isa. 2:12 (cf. Isa. 2:20; 3:17; 5:30; 28:5-6; Amos 2:16; 8:9; Hosea 2:18). See
SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

Conscious creation (humans and angels) will one day stand before its Creator and give
account of the stewardship of the gift of life (i.e. Matt. 25:31-46; Rev. 20:11-15). YHWH is a moral, ethical God;
creation is a moral, ethical creation. Humans do not break God's laws so much as break themselves on God's laws.
The laws are for our protection in a fallen world, but humans see them as restrictions and loss of personal freedoms.
One day every conscious creation, human and angel, will give an account before God (cf. Phil. 2:9-11)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: JUDGMENT IN THE NT

verses.zh: 必有万军耶和华降罚的一个日子，要临到骄傲狂妄的；一切自高的都必降为卑；
verses.en: Indeed, the Lord of Heaven’s Armies has planned a day of judgment[NOTE:1] for[NOTE:2] all the high and mighty;for all who are proud—they will be humiliated;
notes: Heb “indeed [or “for”] the Lord of Heaven’s Armies [traditionally, “the Lord of hosts”] has a day.”
Or “against” (NAB, NASB, NRSV).
verses.commentary:
2:12-13 Notice the recurrent use of terms denoting arrogant, prideful humans and nations.

- "everyone who is proud" (BDB 144, KB 168), Isa. 2:12.

- "and lofty" (BDB 926, KB 1202, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE (note the
same form in Isa. 2:13, 14), Isa. 2:12

- "everyone who is lifted up" (BDB 669, KB 724, Niphal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE
(note the same form in Isa. 2:13,14), Isa. 2:12

- "all the cedars of Lebanon that are lofty and lifted up," Isa. 2:13 (imagery for proud humans and nations)

2:12 "For the Lord of hosts will have a day of reckoning" This does not follow
the Hebrew text. The MT has "For the day of the Lord of hosts" (cf. NKJV). The
NASB translation is trying to link this back to Isa. 1:18.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DAY OF THE LORD

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

▣ Notice the two types of parallelism in v. 12. Lines 2 and 3 are in a synonymous parallelism,
while line 4 is in an antithetical parallelism to them.

One day the pride of wicked leaders and the wealthy will be brought low (cf. v. 11).

2:12-16 Note the repeated use of "against" (BDB 752, KB 825).

- against everyone who is proud and lofty, Isa. 2:12

- against all that is lifted up, Isa. 2:12

- against all the cedars of Lebanon that are lofty and lifted up, Isa. 2:13

- against all the oaks of Bashan (who are also lofty and lifted up), Isa. 2:13

- against all the lofty mountains, Isa. 2:14

- against all the hills that are lifted up, Isa. 2:14

- against every high tower, Isa. 2:15

- against every fortified wall, Isa. 2:15

- against all the ships of Tarshish, Isa. 2:16

- against all beautiful craft, Isa. 2:16 (this word "craft" [BDB 967] appears only here and its
meaning is uncertain; it may parallel "ships of Tarshish" in Isa. 2:16a)

The Lord opposes the proud (cf. Isa. 2:11 and 17).

verses.zh: 又临到黎巴嫩高大的香柏树和巴珊的橡树；
verses.en: for all the cedars of Lebanonthat are so high and mighty,for all the oaks of Bashan,[NOTE:1]
notes: The cedars of Lebanon and oaks of Bashan were well-known for their size and prominence. They make apt symbols here for powerful men who think of themselves as prominent and secure.
verses.commentary:
2:13 Because of the allusion to idolatry with trees (Isa. 1:29) and gardens (Isa. 1:29-30) and that
YHWH will burn them, one wonders if this mention of lofty trees reflects

- the pride and arrogance of nations

- the worship of idols connected with trees/wood

Because of the larger context (i.e. "against" series) the first option seems best. The problem of
human pride is summarized in Isa. 2:17 (which may be the theme of the entire book).

SPECIAL TOPIC: TREES

verses.zh: 又临到一切高山的峻岭；
verses.en: for all the tall mountains,for all the high hills,[NOTE:1]
notes: The high mountains and hills symbolize the apparent security of proud men, as do the high tower and fortified wall of v. 15.

verses.zh: 又临到高台和坚固城墙；
verses.en: for every high tower,for every fortified wall,

verses.zh: 又临到他施的船只并一切可爱的美物。
verses.en: for all the large ships,[NOTE:1] for all the impressive[NOTE:2] ships.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “the ships of Tarshish.” This probably refers to large ships either made in or capable of traveling to the distant western port of Tarshish.
Heb “desirable”; NAB, NIV “stately”; NRSV “beautiful.”

The ships mentioned in this verse were the best of their class, and therefore an apt metaphor for the proud men being denounced in this speech.tn On the meaning of this word, which appears only here in the Hebrew Bible, see H. R. Cohen, Biblical Hapax Legomena (SBLDS), 41-42.

2:16 "all the ships of Tarshish" See note at Isa. 23:1.

verses.zh: 骄傲的必屈膝；狂妄的必降卑。在那日，惟独耶和华被尊崇；
verses.en: Proud men will be humiliated,arrogant men will be brought low;[NOTE:1] the Lord alone will be exalted[NOTE:2] in that day.
notes: Heb “and the pride of men will be brought down, and the arrogance of men will be brought low.” As in v. 11, the repetition of the verbs שָׁפַל (shafal) and שָׁחָח (shakhakh) from v. 9 draws attention to the appropriate nature of the judgment. Those proud men who “bow low” before idols will be forced to “bow low” before God when he judges their sin.
Or “elevated”; NCV “praised”; CEV “honored.”
verses.commentary:
2:17 This is parallel in thought to Isa. 2:11, which is the opposite of what evil leaders and
wealthy socialites had done to the poor and humble in Isa. 2:9. Many see this verse as a summary theme
of the entire book (Jewish Study Bible, p. 788)!

verses.zh: 偶像必全然废弃。
verses.en: The worthless idols will be completely eliminated.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “will completely pass away”; ASV “shall utterly pass away.” tc The verb “pass away” is singular in the Hebrew text, despite the plural subject (“worthless idols”) that precedes. The verb should be emended to a plural; the final vav (ו) has been accidentally omitted by haplography (note the vav at the beginning of the immediately following form).
verses.commentary:
2:18 Idolatry will cease completely (cf. Isa. 21:9) because the worship of them is "emptiness"
(cf. Isa. 30:22; 31:7; 40:18-20; 44:9-20; 46:5-7)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

verses.zh: 耶和华兴起，使地大震动的时候，人就进入石洞，进入土穴，躲避耶和华的惊吓和他威严的荣光。
verses.en: They[NOTE:1] will go into caves in the rocky cliffsand into holes in the ground[NOTE:2] trying to escape the dreadful judgment of the Lord[NOTE:3] and his royal splendor,when he rises up to terrify the earth.[NOTE:4]
notes: The identity of the grammatical subject is unclear. The “idols” could be the subject; they will “go” into the caves and holes when the idolaters throw them there in their haste to escape God’s judgment (see vv. 20-21). The picture of the idols, which represent the foreign deities worshiped by the people, fleeing from the Lord would be highly polemical and fit the overall mood of the chapter. However it seems more likely that the idolaters themselves are the subject, for v. 10 uses similar language in sarcastically urging them to run from judgment.
Heb “dust”; ASV “into the holes of the earth.”
Heb “from the dread of the Lord,” that is, from the dread that he produces in the objects of his judgment.” The words “trying to escape” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Or “land.” It is not certain if these verses are describing the judgment of Judah (see vv. 6-9) or a more universal judgment on all proud men.
verses.commentary:
2:19 "When He arises to make the earth tremble" The first VERBAL "arise"
(BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) can denote

- appear on the scene, Exod. 1:8; Deut. 34:10; Jdg. 5:7; 2 Kgs. 23:25

- arise for action (from His throne), Num. 10:35; 2 Chr. 6:41; Job 31:14; Ps. 76:9; 132:8

The second VERBAL "tremble" (BDB 791, KB 888, Qal
INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) describes physical creation as its Creator approaches
(cf. Isa. 13:13; 24:1,19,20; Ps. 18:7; 68:7-8; Hag. 2:6; also note Rom. 8:19). YHWH can come for
blessing or judgment. In this context it is for judgment!

verses.zh: 到那日，人必将为拜而造的金偶像、银偶像抛给田鼠和蝙蝠。
verses.en: At that time[NOTE:1] men will throw their silver and gold idols,which they made for themselves to worship,[NOTE:2] into the caves where rodents and bats live,[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “in that day” (KJV).
Or “bow down to.”

Heb “to the shrews and to the bats.” On the meaning of חֲפַרְפָּרָה (khafarparah, “shrew”), see HALOT 341 s.v. חֲפַרְפָּרָה. The BHS text as it stands (פֵּרוֹת לַחְפֹּר, perot lakhpor), makes no sense. Based on Theodotion’s transliteration and a similar reading in the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa, most scholars suggest that the MT mistakenly divided a noun (a hapax legomenon) that should be translated “moles,” “shrews,” or “rodents.”
verses.commentary:
2:20-21 To clarify the first line of Isa. 2:10, humans will try to hide from God

- in caves in the rocks (cf. Isa. 2:21)

- in manmade tunnels

They will try to get rid of their precious idols

- cast away to moles (NASB, Peshitta; the meaning of the word is uncertain)

- LXX has "vanities"

- REB has "dung-beetles"

- JPSOA has "flying foxes" (a type of bat, therefore, parallel to the next line of poetry)

It is related to the VERB "to dig" (BDB 343), therefore, to
animals that dig or live in the ground

- NET has "rodents"

- cast away to bats

These two verses have a series of INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS.

- to the moles (lit. "to dig"), BDB 343, KB 340, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT

- to worship (lit, "bow down"), BDB 1005, KB 295, Hishtaphel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT

- to go into, BDB 97, KB 112, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT

- arises, BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT, same form
as Isa. 2:19 (line 5)

- tremble (lit. "to frighten," BDB 791, KB 888, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT,
same as Isa. 2:19 (line 5)

In the IVP Bible Background Commentary "a Sumerian Hymn of Enheduanna to the
goddess Inanna from the third millennium depicts gods fluttering away like bats to their caves from the
goddess's terrible presence" (p. 588). This means that it must remain a possibility that it is the idols
themselves that were carried down by insects (beetles) or digging animals seeking refuge from the coming
of YHWH because they could not move themselves.

verses.zh: 到耶和华兴起，使地大震动的时候，人好进入磐石洞中和岩石穴里，躲避耶和华的惊吓和他威严的荣光。
verses.en: so they themselves can go into the crevices of the rocky cliffsand the openings under the rocky overhangs,[NOTE:1] trying to escape the dreadful judgment of the Lord[NOTE:2] and his royal splendor,when he rises up to terrify the earth.[NOTE:3]
notes: The precise point of vv. 20-21 is not entirely clear. Are they taking the idols into their hiding places with them because they are so attached to their man-made images? Or are they discarding the idols along the way as they retreat into the darkest places they can find? In either case it is obvious that the gods are incapable of helping them.
Heb “from the dread of the Lord,” that is, from the dread that he produces in the objects of his judgment.” The words “trying to escape” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

Or “land.” It is not certain if these verses are describing the judgment of Judah (see vv. 6-9) or a more universal judgment on all proud men. Almost all English versions translate “earth,” taking this to refer to universal judgment.

verses.zh: 你们休要倚靠世人。他鼻孔里不过有气息；他在一切事上可算甚么呢？
verses.en: Stop trusting in human beings,whose life’s breath is in their nostrils.For why should they be given special consideration?
verses.commentary:
2:22 The VERBAL PHRASE "stop regarding" (Qal IMPERATIVE
and a Niphal PARTICIPLE) is emphatic! Some humans trust in themselves (cf. Ps. 146:3; Jer. 17:5)
and not YHWH. Faithful followers should not give a thought to them! They look prosperous and happy, but their day
will come when they stand before God in judgment, both in time and at the end of time.

READING CYCLE THREE (see
"Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you
are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You,
the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject
divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the
original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- Isaiah 2 begins with another introductory phrase, like Isa. 1:1. It is possible that editors
or compilers put Isaiah's sermons/visions/messages together based on

- chronology (under which king)

- topic

- catch words

- unknown literary scheme

- a written copy of several Isaiah messages

See note in The Jewish Study Bible, p. 787.

- This chapter is typical of the prophet's messages.

- hope for all nations through YHWH's covenant people (Isa. 2:2-4)

- judgment for covenant violations and wickedness (Isa. 2:5-22; note Lev. 26 and Deut. 28)

- YHWH wants a righteous, holy, covenant people to reflect His character to the
nations so that they can respond to Him in faith and righteousness (cf. Isa. 45:22;
49:6; 60:3; 66:18,23).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

- Remember in these poetic literary units (visions), do not push the details or single
lexical studies, but the overall pattern of parallelism, word plays, and contrasts! The
whole poem is meant to convey one major truth! Be careful of picking and choosing
themes, words, or truths you are comfortable with or that fit you're á priori
systematic theology. Let Isaiah speak!

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

- Because of the unifying theme of Jerusalem (judged and blessed), Isaiah 2-4 forms
a literary unit.

- A book that has helped me understand the language of prophecy and apocalyptic
is D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language
of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic, IVP, ISBN 0-83-8-2653-X.

- Series of woes, Isa. 2:8-23

- Judgment, Isa. 2:24-30

- natural, Isa. 2:25

- invader, Isa. 2:26-30
